newsitem.title: USA: Wholesale prices fall 0.3 percent in January.
newsitem.headline: Wholesale prices fall 0.3 percent in January.

text.p: Wholesale prices retreated for the first time in more than two years in January, the government said Friday, surprising Wall Street and suggesting that inflationary pressures remain largely contained despite the continuing economic expansion.
The Labour Department said the Producer Price Index fell 0.3 percent last month, after rising a revised 0.6 percent in December.

However, the so-called core rate, which excludes the often-volatile food and energy sectors, was unchanged in January after rising 0.1 percent in December. Economists believe this more closely tracks the pattern of inflation.
The decline in the January PPI was not expected by Wall Street, which had forecast an overall increase of 0.3 percent, with the core rate up 0.2 percent.
"Whoosh! It almost leaves you speechless," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany. "It doesn't say much for forecasters.
"Despite the fact that the economy has been recovering since March of 1991, there are still very few signs of upward pressure on prices," he added. "That's very, very unusual."
Michael Moran of Daiwa Securities agreed that the performance was altogether remarkable at a time when the economic expansion was nearly six years old.
But he said there was still some indication in other economic measures, such as average hourly wages and the wage component of the employment cost index, suggesting some inflationary pressures.
"Economic theory that shows increased inflationary pressures building as the expansion matures has not been turned totally on its head," Moran said. "Still, it's a remarkable showing."
Word of the drop in wholesale prices, the first since a 0.4 percent decline in October 1994, was followed by a Federal Reserve report showing a leveling off of industrial production in January.
The Fed said production by the nation's mines, factories and utilities was unchanged last month after climbing by a revised 0.5 percent in December and by 0.8 percent in November.
The leveling off in output further reduces inflationary pressures on the economy, according to analysts.

"The production index for business equipment rose further in January, but the indexes for consumer goods and for materials were little changed," the Fed said. "The output of construction supplies fell for a second month."
The Labour Department's tame inflation report showed energy prices declined 0.2 percent last month after jumping 3.4 percent in December.
Gasoline prices, however, rose 2.6 percent, although this was offset by a 2.8 percent decline in home heating oil.
Food prices also moved lower, by 1.0 percent, as meat and fruit costs declined.
Tobacco costs edged up 0.1 percent, while passenger car prices dropped 0.4 percent after a 0.1 percent increase in December.
Goods at the intermediate level of production, which require additional processing, rose 0.2 percent after gaining 0.3 percent in December.

Prices at the early part of the production cycle, so-called crude goods, jumped 5.2 percent after being up 4.9 percent in December, which economists said bore further watching although this is often a volatile number.
The department previously reported that overall prices rose 0.5 percent in December.

Separately, the Department of Commerce reported Friday that inventories held by businesses declined slightly in December as fewer goods remained on the shelves of manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers.

Total business inventories fell a slight 0.1 percent in December to a seasonally adjusted $1.01 trillion after being revised to show no change in November. Previously, the department said inventories had risen 0.1 percent in November.
